Pull request description:

  This is split off from #36521. This PR focuses on reducing memory usage of transactions in memory, leaving performance improvements for other PRs.

  `CScriptWitness` stores a witness stack as a `std::vector<std::vector<unsigned char>>`, which costs a 24-byte vector object and an allocation for every non-empty element. This makes it possible to construct transactions that take a large amount of memory after deserialization.

  This PR first introduces encapsulation for `CScriptWitness`, hiding its representation. The last commit then changes the representation to be single `std::unique_ptr<byte[]>` which for non-empty witness stacks stores their serialization prefixed by a small length header. Witnesses can no longer be modified in place; they can only be replaced in their entirety. Access to the individual witness stack elements is done by on-the-fly deserialization instead.

  `CScriptWitness` shrinks from 24 to 8 bytes, and `CTxIn` from 112 to 96 bytes. Worst-case allocated size for transactions kept in memory drops from roughly 28 bytes/WU to 1.6 bytes/WU.

  This worsens deserialization and validation time, adding some 50-70 ms per block to the worst case for me. A follow-up #36918 with optimizations improves the worst case deserialization time significantly instead. Other minor degradations:
  * libbitcoinkernel's witness stack element accessor becomes $\mathcal{O}(n)$ in the index of the witness element; using it to iterate a whole witness may therefore become $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$.
  * `CScriptWitness::back()` is $\mathcal{O}(n)$ in the length of the witness stack.

  Issue reported by furszy and 0xB10C.

Merge bitcoin/bitcoin#36716: net: only monitor select exceptions while connecting

97e3c9562291f5bbc2b03fef1c70e4975eb2a8c6 net: only use the select error set while connecting (Sjors Provoost)

Pull request description:

  Alternative approach to #36688, citing the relevant parts of its description:

  > There is currently nothing preventing us to receive TCP urgent data, which would never be returned by `recv()`. Linux's `poll()` is indifferent to this, but the `select()` socket monitoring may keep reporting it as pending on some platforms.
  >
  > This would not prevent progress nor lead to a crash anymore after #36665, but it's still undesirable.

  Fix this by only adding a socket to the `select()` exception set while waiting for a non-blocking `connect()` to complete. Windows needs that to detect a failed connection. Established connections no longer monitor the exception set on any platform. This approach was suggested by theuni in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36716#issuecomment-6931290348.

  To opt in, `ErrorEvent` can now be requested from `Sock::Wait()`, like `RecvEvent` and `SendEvent`. With `select()` that adds the socket to the exception set. `ConnectToSocket()` is the only caller that requests it. There is no behavior change with `poll()`, which reports errors whether or not they are requested. Using `ErrorEvent` for this was suggested by vasild in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36716#discussion_r4692637894.

  We could instead have set `SO_OOBINLINE` on our sockets, so `recv()` returns any urgent data sent to us (and likely leads us to disconnect the peer). RFC 6093 doesn't forbid this, but the current approach seems more clear and direct to me.

  A new unit test in `sock_tests` covers the fix itself: with an urgent byte pending, waiting for `RecvEvent` must not report `ErrorEvent`. Without the fix it fails on a `select()` build.

  Backports until 29.x are straight-forward, but for 31.x and before require compensating for the scripted-diff in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/f395acdeeeaa1f3fd75d3cedbf2731fa24083e9f.

Merge bitcoin/bitcoin#34193: wallet: make migration more robust against failures

399a5a3805884e7ac5a2cbdf616be8c9041bc2bd test: migrate a wallet with a leftover journal at its location (furszy)
42131a81fdc42ab0cb295a2267ce33e9fb8221ff test: migrate wallet located on a different filesystem (furszy)
b8ef499909b09f9dffa32172912c1e37f2e78867 wallet: migration, make sqlite creation robust against failures (furszy)
e3a5a48a03565696947be3ff3516ae013d4fd658 wallet: migration, add MigrationFilePrefix() helper (Ryan Ofsky)
b6b2f9f12b13e429a8511130bdcdc7075adbc28e wallet: use RunWithinTxn within MigrateToSQLite (furszy)
cf5e6803f07d1bfc6ae7ac655e7063c650bcb2f8 wallet: fail migration gracefully on non-writable wallets (furszy)
84a9f486475de9fab0b5cc8ab7b0338e04117163 wallet: migration, restore backup if an exception is thrown (furszy)
3a9ba874bb7efab4401d86a073964774f88de393 wallet: migration, handle exceptions during wallet creation (furszy)
edbf3b62a2cb258bb585045c769b1215c577e8e1 wallet: migration, unify watchonly and solvables wallets creation (furszy)

Pull request description:

  This is just me finding a few more edge cases after #34156 and #34176

  The goal of the PR is to handle failures in a controlled way. Just so the process can automatically restore the original wallet without requiring user manual intervention.

  The covered cases are:

  1. During `DoMigration()`: There are methods that can throw exceptions and abruptly abort the process. 
  Instead of crashing (GUI) or returning a generic exception, we now will catch and return the error gracefully. This lets the process restore the original wallet automatically.

  2. Trying to migrate a wallet in a read-only directory throws a filesystem exception and skips cleanup.
   Now the process will fail gracefully with a clear error msg, and automatically restore the original wallet.

  3. Any failure during `MigrateToSQLite` requires user manual intervention. 
  Now the original wallet db will remain untouched, and only be updated once the sqlite db creation fully succeeds.

  ryanofsky:
    Code review ACK 399a5a3805884e7ac5a2cbdf616be8c9041bc2bd. This is a clear improvement over master, which deletes the original database before writing the new one and asserts if anything fails after that. Now the new database is fully built before it replaces the original, failures after that point restore the backup, and a leftover journal at the wallet location stops the migration instead of corrupting the new database.

Merge bitcoin/bitcoin#35765: depends: keep local source archives in WORK_PATH

01491f22b2c77d632e8503cc446140d1ab6ccc21 depends: store local package tarballs in WORK_PATH instead of SOURCES_PATH (Ryan Ofsky)

Pull request description:

  Local package tarballs are generated from the current checkout, but depends caches them alongside downloaded archives in `SOURCES_PATH`. When checkouts share that directory, a cached local tarball can be newer than another checkout's source files, causing depends to build the wrong sources with a valid checksum and build ID.

  Store local package tarballs and their checksum stamps in `WORK_PATH/local-sources` instead. `WORK_PATH` is per-checkout by default, so generated snapshots stay with their checkout while downloaded sources remain shareable through `SOURCES_PATH`. Existing mtime-based invalidation is unchanged.

  This also handles `contrib/guix/guix-build`, which mounts each checkout at `/bitcoin`. Distinguishing local tarballs by absolute source path cannot isolate those builds when `SOURCES_PATH` is shared.

  Validation: focused checks reproduced the same-path collision with the path-hash approach and verified isolation with this change. Host/container source checksums and build IDs match; archive reuse, refresh after an edit, and downloaded-source paths were also checked. No full Guix build was run.

  Addresses #35764.

Merge bitcoin/bitcoin#36709: guix: compute --build triplet when lowering, not at load time

d7a8360f4ef5ff90b71d87b15ec4c5048b9ea0a9 guix: compute --build triplet when lowering, not at load time (Jorge Espada)

Pull request description:

  ### Why

  `building-on` in `contrib/guix/toolchains.scm` reads `(%current-system)` once, when the module is loaded. `guix shell` loads the manifest before it applies `--system`, so the value is the system of the machine that runs the build, not the system that Guix builds for.

  So a build with `ADDITIONAL_GUIX_ENVIRONMENT_FLAGS="--system=aarch64-linux"` on an x86_64 machine (for example with `qemu-binfmt-service-type`, to get an aarch64 build machine) configures the aarch64 cross toolchain with `--build=x86_64-guix-linux-gnu`. `gcc-cross-sans-libc` then fails to configure:

  ```
  checking for CET support... configure: error: compiler and assembler with CET support are required for --enable-cet
  ```

  ### What changes

  `building-on` becomes a procedure, and its three call sites call it. Guix then computes the triplet for each derivation, under the system that the derivation is built for.

  ### How I checked

  - On master, `HOST=x86_64-linux-gnu guix shell -n --system=aarch64-linux -m contrib/guix/linux_static.scm` (with `toolchains.scm` on the load path, as `guix-build` does) gives `gcc-cross-sans-libc` with `--build=x86_64-guix-linux-gnu`. With this PR it gives `--build=aarch64-guix-linux-gnu`. That is the same derivation that `guix build -d --system=aarch64-linux` gives on master.
  - Native builds (no `--system`): the toolchain derivations from `linux_static.scm` and `manifest_gui.scm` are identical on master and with this PR. So this PR does not change release builds.
  - With this PR, an emulated aarch64 build of `x86_64-linux-gnu` on x86_64 built the whole cross toolchain and the non-GUI binaries. The GUI environment then failed in the tests of `python-pylint` (timeout under emulation) and `maturin` (snapshot mismatch). These packages have no aarch64 substitutes at the pinned Guix commit, and the failures are not related to this change.

net: only use the select error set while connecting

Windows uses the select() error set to report a failed non-blocking
connect(). Make ErrorEvent an event that can be requested from
Sock::Wait(), like RecvEvent and SendEvent: with select() it adds the
socket to the error set. ConnectToSocket() requests it while
connecting. This is safe on all platforms, as any error condition is
worth waking for there.

All other uses of select() now leave the error set empty. With
select(), sockets waited on without ErrorEvent no longer wake up for
or report exceptional conditions, such as TCP urgent data on an
established connection. No behavior change with poll().

Add a unit test: with an urgent byte pending, waiting for RecvEvent
must not report ErrorEvent.

  - `descriptor_tests`: `DoCheck` built the spending transaction with `vin.resize(1)` / `vout.resize(1)` and then wrote `nSequence` through `vin[0]`. It now uses literal `vin`/`vout` lists, which also makes the default input and the empty output visible.

commit.message:
doc: add release note for the reduced memory usage of witnesses

Storing witness stacks in serialized form reduces the memory that
transactions use, so the mempool can hold more of them within the
same -maxmempool limit.

script: store witness stacks as their serialization

Replace CScriptWitness's vector of vectors with a single allocation,
containing the size of the stack's serialization (4 bytes, little
endian), followed by that serialization. An empty stack uses no
allocation at all.

This means a witness stack no longer needs one allocation per non-empty
element plus one for the outer vector, and no longer has a 24-byte
overhead per element. A block whose witnesses consist of millions of
tiny elements thus no longer costs tens of bytes of memory and an
allocation per byte. It also shrinks CScriptWitness from 24 to 8 bytes,
and thus CTxIn from 112 to 96 bytes. The downside is that indexing
becomes O(n) in the distance from the bottom of the stack.

This is the simplest implementation of this representation:
deserialization still goes through a vector of vectors, and elements
are found by parsing the serialization with SpanReader and
ReadCompactSize. Both can be made faster in follow-up changes.

span: add SameSpan

Add a helper that tells whether two spans refer to the same range of
memory, rather than whether their contents are equal. A future commit
uses it to compare iterators that consist of a span.

script: remove CScriptWitness's old interface

All users of CScriptWitness now go through the interface that hides its
representation. Make the stack vector private, turning the struct into a
class, and remove IsNull() and SetNull(), which have no callers left.

The representation itself does not change here.

test, bench, fuzz: build witness stacks before constructing a CScriptWitness

Convert the remaining uses of CScriptWitness::stack in tests, benchmarks,
and fuzz tests, by constructing witnesses from a separately-built vector
of elements, rather than modifying the stack in place.

refactor: use CScriptWitness's interface where that needs more than a rename

Convert the remaining non-test uses of CScriptWitness::stack, which need
more than a substitution.

This includes the range-based for loops over the stack. Iterating over a
CScriptWitness yields its elements as spans, by value, where the stack's
elements were vectors bound by reference. The spans refer to memory
owned by the witness, so they stay valid as long as it is not modified.

policy: iterate over witness stacks directly in IsWitnessStandard

Instead of indexing into the witness stack for the P2WSH checks, and
popping elements off a span of it for the Taproot checks, iterate over
the elements of the witness, and look up its last element only once.
This no longer needs the stack as a vector, and avoids indexing, which
will not be constant-time once witnesses are stored in serialized form.

In the P2WSH checks, look at the number of elements before the size of
the last one, so that a stack with too many elements is rejected
without finding its last element, which will not be constant-time
either.

script: build the witness execution stack with ToVectors()

VerifyWitnessProgram used a span over CScriptWitness::stack, popped the
elements with other roles (the witness script, the annex, the control
block, and the leaf script) off that span, and copied the remaining
elements into the initial execution stack.

Instead, convert the witness to a vector of vectors once, using
ToVectors(), pop those elements off that vector, and move what remains
into the execution stack.

script: let ExecuteWitnessScript take its initial stack by value

This lets callers move the stack into it, rather than having it be
copied from a span. This will be used in a future commit.

scripted-diff: replace witnesses as a whole instead of their stack

Convert the uses of CScriptWitness::stack (and SetNull()) that clear the
stack, assign a new one, or push a single element onto an empty one, to
assigning a new witness. The remaining uses are converted manually in
the next commits.

-BEGIN VERIFY SCRIPT-
FILES=$(git grep -l -E '\.stack\b|(scriptWitness|final_script_witness)\.SetNull\(\)' -- src ':!src/script/miniscript.*' ':!src/script/script.h')

# Clearing the stack (SetNull(), clear() or resize(0)): assign an empty
# witness. A clear() followed by pushing elements in a loop is left for
# the manual changes.
sed -i -E -e '/txin\.scriptWitness\.stack\.clear/b' \
    -e 's/(scriptWitness|final_script_witness)\.SetNull\(\)/\1 = {}/' \
    -e 's/(scriptWitness)\.stack\.(clear\(\)|resize\(0\));$/\1 = {};/' $FILES

# Assigning a vector of elements to the stack: assign a witness
# constructed from it (moving from the vector is pointless, as the
# witness is constructed from a const reference). An assignment that
# spells out the vector's type is left for the manual changes.
sed -i -E -e '/\.stack = std::vector</b' \
    -e 's/(\w+)\.stack = (std::move\((\w+)\)|(.*));$/\1 = CScriptWitness{\3\4};/' $FILES

# Pushing a single element onto an empty witness (in these benchmarks
# and tests): assign a witness constructed from that element. The one
# place that pushes onto a non-empty witness (to make a different
# witness) is left for the manual changes, as are pushes in loops.
sed -i -E '/ tx\.vin\[0\]\.scriptWitness\.stack\.push_back\(\{5\}\)|Consume/!s/(\w+)\.stack\.push_back\((.*)\);$/\1 = CScriptWitness{{\2}};/' \
    src/bench/blockencodings.cpp src/bench/mempool_eviction.cpp src/bench/mempool_stress.cpp src/bench/rpc_mempool.cpp \
    src/test/fuzz/connect_block.cpp src/test/fuzz/txdownloadman.cpp src/test/orphanage_tests.cpp src/test/txdownload_tests.cpp \
    src/test/validation_block_tests.cpp
-END VERIFY SCRIPT-

scripted-diff: serialize CScriptWitness rather than its stack

Convert the uses of CScriptWitness::stack that serialize or deserialize
it, or compute the size of its serialization. The witness itself has the
same serialization as its stack.

-BEGIN VERIFY SCRIPT-
sed -i -E -e 's/ (>>|<<) ([][A-Za-z0-9_.]+)\.stack( <<|;)/ \1 \2\3/' \
    -e 's/(SerializeToVector|UnserializeFromVector)\(s, (\w+)\.stack\)/\1(s, \2)/' \
    -e 's/::GetSerializeSize\(([][A-Za-z0-9_.]+)\.stack\)/::GetSerializeSize(\1)/' \
    $(git grep -l -E '\.stack\b' -- src ':!src/script/miniscript.*' ':!src/script/script.h')
-END VERIFY SCRIPT-

scripted-diff: read and compare CScriptWitness through its interface

Convert the uses of CScriptWitness::stack that read an element by index,
bind a const reference to the stack, or compare two stacks, and the
uses of IsNull().

-BEGIN VERIFY SCRIPT-
FILES=$(git grep -l -E '\.stack\b' -- src ':!src/script/miniscript.*' ':!src/script/script.h')

# Reading an element by index: the witness has operator[] itself. Writes
# to elements, and loops indexing all elements (which can be quadratic
# with indexing that is not constant-time), are left for the manual
# changes.
sed -i -E -e '/MAX_STANDARD_P2WSH_STACK_ITEM_SIZE|HexStr\((txin\.)?scriptWitness\.stack\[|\.stack\[[^]]*\]( =|\.resize)|^\s*\+\+/b' \
    -e 's/\.stack\[/[/g' $FILES

# Const references to the stack: refer to the witness itself, which
# provides the same read-only accessors.
sed -i -E 's/^(\s*const auto& \w+( = |\{).*)\.stack(\}?;)$/\1\3/' $FILES

# Comparisons of two stacks: compare the witnesses, which are equal
# exactly when their stacks are.
sed -i -E '/\.stack [!=]= /s/\.stack\b//g' $FILES

# IsNull(): use empty(), which the witness provides along with size()
# and its other container-like accessors.
sed -i -E -e 's/(scriptWitness|final_script_witness)\.IsNull\(\)/\1.empty()/g' \
    -e 's/witness->IsNull\(\)/witness->empty()/g' \
    $(git grep -l -E '(scriptWitness|final_script_witness)\.IsNull\(\)|witness->IsNull\(\)' -- src)
-END VERIFY SCRIPT-

scripted-diff: use CScriptWitness's size(), empty() and back()

Convert the uses of CScriptWitness::stack that only need the number of
elements, whether there are any, or the last element, which the witness
provides itself. Other uses are converted in the next commits.

-BEGIN VERIFY SCRIPT-
# Lines that need the stack itself (to compute the size of its
# serialization without the element count, to pass the last element
# where a vector is expected, or to index all elements in a loop) are
# left for the manual changes.
sed -i -E -e '/GetSizeOfCompactSize|TAPROOT_LEAF_TAPSCRIPT|i < (txin\.)?scriptWitness\.stack/b' \
    -e 's/\.stack\.(size|empty|back)\(\)/.\1()/g' \
    $(git grep -l -E '\.stack\.(size|empty|back)\(\)' -- src ':!src/script/miniscript.*' ':!src/script/script.h')
-END VERIFY SCRIPT-

test: check CScriptWitness against the vector of vectors it represents

Add a unit test and a fuzz test that compare CScriptWitness's interface
(accessors, construction, and serialization) with the
std::vector<std::vector<unsigned char>> it represents. The unit test
focuses on element counts and sizes around CompactSize encoding
boundaries.

script: give CScriptWitness an interface that hides its representation

Add element access through spans (forward iteration, front(), back(), and
indexing), conversion to and construction from a vector of elements,
serialization, and memory usage accounting, so that users no longer need to
access the stack vector directly. This prepares for a future commit which
will replace the representation with a more compact & efficient one.

The stack vector itself stays public until the next commits have converted
its users.

  **Problem:** The binary verifier counts signatures from expired and revoked keys toward `--min-good-sigs`.

  This was found and disclosed responsibly by the Red Team 🟥.

commit.message:
wallet: migration, make sqlite creation robust against failures

Currently, MigrateToSQLite loads all BDB records into memory,
deletes the original database, creates the sqlite db in its
place, and writes the records to it. If anything fails after the
delete, the wallet is left partly in sqlite format with legacy
records, and the user has to restore the backup manually.

Instead, build the sqlite db in a temporary directory next to the
original db file, and once all records are written, rename it into
place. For wallet directories, the rename atomically replaces the
original wallet.dat, so any earlier failure leaves the original
untouched. A plain file wallet becomes a wallet directory, which
can't replace the file atomically, so the original file is erased
just before the move.

Before the move, check that no other files of the db, such as a
leftover journal, are at the destination, and fail if one is.
SQLite would otherwise roll a leftover journal back into the new
db when opening it, corrupting it.

Failures once the original db may have been erased or replaced
throw, so the migration restores the backup.

commit.message:
wallet: fail migration gracefully on non-writable wallets

Currently, migrating a wallet whose database directory or file
is not writable throws a filesystem exception. Migration
then tries to restore the backup, which also throws again and
the user ends up seeing the raw exception.

Return a regular migration error instead, before the wallet is
modified. The error describes the problem better, and suggests
adjusting the permissions when that is the cause. The wallet
stays as it was, so the migration can be retried once the
problem is fixed without any manual intervention.

wallet is restored from the backup automatically, the same way as when

Merge bitcoin/bitcoin#36908: mining: avoid checkBlock crash when chain has no tip

8cba4bace8df92afcc9ff46404e36c741d557b64 mining: avoid checkBlock crash when chain has no tip (Turtlecute33)

Pull request description:

  **The problem**: `Init.makeMining` returns as soon as the chainstate is loaded. On a first start with an empty datadir, or on a node started with `-reindex`/`-reindex-chainstate`, this is before the genesis block is connected, so the active chain has no tip. A `Mining.checkBlock` call in this window reaches `TestBlockValidity()`, which asserts that the tip exists, and the node aborts.

  **The fix**: in `MakeMining`, if `wait_loaded` is set, wait for the chainstate to be present and for the tip to be non-null.

  *Alternative fix*: In `Mining.checkBlock`, check if the tip is present, return early with "inconclusive-no-chain-tip" otherwise. (I initially implemented this fix, but decided to go with the `makeMining` one instead, see https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36908#discussion_r4610682758)

  The crash can be reproduced on master using the functional test included in this PR.

  This is joint work with Turtlecute33 :)

Pull request description:

  `wallet_keypool_topup.py` is meant to test keypool restore for four output types, one node each. But the wallet and backup paths are only set for node1, so for nodes 2-4 the test copies node1's backup over node1's running wallet and restarts the node under test on its own, never-restored wallet.   Also fixes `wallet_createwallet.py` calling `w7.walletpassphrase` where it means w8 (since c5d3787367), so the `avoid_reuse wallet` was never checked.

bb357fcd2fc55807905868e3c394579306ec4b44 node: move block filter index ownership to NodeContext (woltx)
66892cdd56338c4e780c05cfd8d8045f09a826bb net_processing: get block filter index via PeerManager::Options (woltx)

  This removes the remaining process-global index ownership and stores node-owned indexes in `NodeContext` instead.

  - `g_coin_stats_index`
  - `g_filter_indexes`

  `NodeContext` now owns these index instances, while `node.indexes` remains a non-owning list used for common index startup, shutdown, and `getindexinfo` handling.

  Behavior should be unchanged, apart from the key order in `getindexinfo` output. Indexes are still created from the same startup options, started in the same init step, stopped before destruction, and destroyed while `validation_signals` is still alive so they can unregister safely.

  The block filter index registry is moved to `node/indexes.{h,cpp}` so `index/` code does not depend on `NodeContext`. `PeerManager` receives a small lookup callback instead of reaching into global state.

  - The fifth commit adds a block filter index lookup callback to `PeerManager::Options`, still backed by the global registry.
  - The last commit is the main one to review carefully. It moves block filter index ownership to `NodeContext`, moves the block filter registry to `node/indexes.{h,cpp}`, and points the `PeerManager` lookup at `NodeContext` instead of global state.

Merge bitcoin/bitcoin#36040: Wallet: Don't backdate locktime rbf 596dd6fd88efe92133a34a0ba8d00f5f369a4bfd Test: bumpfee does not backdate the locktime (Biel) b1ddb7d6857668c82efefebe94f6ba224f71ab4a Wallet: Do not allow bumpfee to backdate the replacement transaction locktime (Biel) Pull request description: Closes https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/26526 Currently, in Bitcoin Core, given an original transaction A and its replacement B, we refer to **backdating** when the locktime of A is higher than the locktime of B (`A.locktime > B.locktime`). This can happen because Bitcoin Core enables **anti-fee-sniping** by default, which sets the transaction's locktime to the current block height. For privacy, 10% of the time, it instead sets a different locktime, randomly chosen between the current height and the current height minus 100 blocks. This can lead into having a replacement of a transaction with a locktime older than its original transaction. This is unrealistics and can be used as a wallet fingerprint. You can find a functional test to reproduce the behaviour mentioned [here](https://gist.github.com/Bicaru20/9afcb878dd103369255cd81cffac86ba) The approach proposed in this PR adds a new parameter to `CoinControl` to keep track of the previous locktime in the case of a `bumpfee`. We then pass this parameter to the DiscourageFeeSniping function through a new parameter, `minimum_height`, whose default value is set to 0.
Alternative approach: Since the locktime of the new transaction is 0, we also considered setting it to the previous locktime value and then, inside `DiscourageFeeSniping`, saving the previous locktime and setting the transaction's locktime to the block height before applying any of the backdating logic. This way, we could avoid passing a new parameter to the function. We ultimately decided not to go with this approach, as it makes the code more difficult to follow.
The only RPC that is affected by this changes is `bumpfee`. The pr also includes a functional test in `wallet_bumpfee.py` to test that when replacing a transation using `bumpfee` the locktime is not backdated.
We also conducted a small analysis to see how many the backdating in RBF transactions actually happen. We have data on the replaced transactions from 2025-05-01 to 2026-06-01. With that we have been able to detect this many backdatings: _We took the date of the last transaction of the replacement chain (A replacement chain are all the transactions that replace themselves)_ In total we have over 1,000,000 rbf transactions, but we see that on average there are only about 200-300 hundred replaccements backdating per week. Looking at the percentages we see that on average is less than 2% of all the transactions that have been replaced. So, it is clear that backdating in replacement transactions is unusual. However, the few transactions that do exhibit backdating are easily fingerprintable as having been replaced using `bumpfee` in Bitcoin Core or Electrum.

Merge bitcoin/bitcoin#36342: wallet: reject recipient amounts above MAX_MONEY

bab579e56aa8b80a6f2923285e55cbcb2a7730b8 wallet: reject recipient amounts outside MoneyRange (Bruce0X)

Pull request description:

  `CreateTransaction` checks that recipient amounts aren't negative, but not that they're within `MAX_MONEY`. `CreateTransactionInternal` then sums them into `recipients_sum` (spend.cpp:1100) with no range check, and that sum can overflow.

  Easiest way to hit it is `fundrawtransaction` with a raw tx that has two outputs of 2^62 sat. It can also be reached with only valid amounts through `walletcreatefundedpsbt`/`send`/`sendmany` and a few thousand 21M BTC outputs. The "Transaction too large" check only runs after coin selection, so it doesn't stop this. On master the node aborts:

  ```
  Assertion failed: (!m_selected_inputs.empty()), function RecalculateWaste, file coinselection.cpp, line 904.
  ```

  UBSan reports the overflow at spend.cpp:1100 first. With other values the sum wraps to a small positive number instead, and `fundrawtransaction` returns success for a tx with outputs of 46116860184 BTC each.

  This checks every amount and the running sum against `MoneyRange` in the existing recipients loop of `CreateTransactionInternal`, before the amount is added to `recipients_sum`, and returns "Transaction output amount must be valid" before coin selection starts. The same check rejects negative amounts, so the separate negative check in `CreateTransaction` is removed. The new `test_outputs_above_max_money` in `wallet_fundrawtransaction.py` covers a single output above MAX_MONEY, two outputs whose sum is above it, a sum that overflows int64, and a negative output. On master the first case returns "Insufficient funds" and the overflow case crashes the node; with the fix all of them get the new error. `wallet_fundrawtransaction.py`, `wallet_send.py`, `wallet_basic.py` and `rpc_psbt.py` pass.

  Assertion failed: (!m_selected_inputs.empty()), function RecalculateWaste, file coinselection.cpp, line 904.

  UBSan reports the overflow at spend.cpp:1100 first. With other values the sum wraps to a small positive number instead, and `fundrawtransaction` returns success for a tx with outputs of 46116860184 BTC each.

  This checks every amount and the running sum against `MoneyRange` in the existing recipients loop of `CreateTransactionInternal`, before the amount is added to `recipients_sum`, and returns "Transaction output amount must be valid" before coin selection starts. The same check rejects negative amounts, so the separate negative check in `CreateTransaction` is removed. The new `test_outputs_above_max_money` in `wallet_fundrawtransaction.py` covers a single output above MAX_MONEY, two outputs whose sum is above it, a sum that overflows int64, and a negative output. On master the first case returns "Insufficient funds" and the overflow case crashes the node; with the fix all of them get the new error. `wallet_fundrawtransaction.py`, `wallet_send.py`, `wallet_basic.py` and `rpc_psbt.py` pass.

Pull request description:

  For more context, see: #36027

  Encrypting existing wallets that are unencrypted is fraught with footguns and complexity both for users and for developers.

  For example:

  - No efforts are made to ensure that remnants of unencrypted key material are not left on the user's disk, as attempting to ensure this would be difficult and dangerous, and for some SSD's infeasible.

  - Encrypting a wallet that has manually imported descriptors will cause the wallet to change the spending conditions out from under the user. (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/26607)

  - Because new keys are made after encryption, restoring from a backup made before encryption may result in loss of funds.

  _LLM Disclosure: Used gemma4-26B and qwen3.8-next-flash as research and drafting tools, but all code and text present here were written by me._

Merge bitcoin/bitcoin#36501: refactor : Reorder CBlockIndex members to save 8 bytes

14edee63b643a96d7588897f0d00002228082178 Reorder CBlockIndex members to save 8 bytes (bartoli)

Pull request description:

  It seems we can save 8 bytes per CBlockIndex instance by reordering one class member. Moving one 8-byte field seems to avoid losing 2x 4 bytes to structure padding on a 64-bit build (on a 32-bit build, there is no gain).

  I could not exactly measure the runtime gain from just this (smaller than RAM usage variation between 2 launches), but I confirmed there was about as many instances of CBlockIndex as blocks in the chain (increasing CBlockIndex size by 320 bytes increases RAM usage by ~300MB), so saving 8 bytes per instance should save about 8MB of RAM at current block height.

  The gain is small, but it seems like it has no cost/risk, since that structure is not used for serialization, and just reordering here should have no side effects.

  I saw a few other types that could gain a few bytes in size by doing something similar (for example, CTxIn), but they have far fewer instances in memory to make the change worth it.

fa1c93477e6ac332219af3eb4c6a5fcc9434105d refactor: Replace unreachable run-time assert with compile time assert (MarcoFalke)

Pull request description:

  The current code uses assertions with falsy literal values in a few places. This is perfectly fine, but this comes with a bit of confusion sometimes:

  * `assert(false)` may cause confusion when it is unclear if `NDEBUG` can disable it. (The intention is to disallow `NDEBUG` compilation). Also, it can lead to warnings when used with clang-cl.exe (GCC seems to understand it)
  * `Assert(false)` hides the noreturn attribute behind a function call, which may cause GCC return-type warnings. (Clang seems to understand it)

  See https://godbolt.org/z/h7PT3jh3Y for the clang-cl/GCC warning reproducer.

  * When C++23 will be allowed, devs may prefer `std::unreachable`. However, this is unsafe and will invoke UB.
  * There is confusion why a `CHECK_NONFATAL` macro exists, but no fatal equivalent.

  Fix all those issues by:

  * Adding a new `AssertUnreachable`, which directly calls the noreturn `internal_abort_helper` helper.
  * Adding an `assert_falsy` linter to enforce code to use this macro.

wallet: rpc: Deprecate `encryptwallet`

Encrypting wallets from creation will still be supported, but there are
footguns both for users and for developers in supporting wallets that
are created unencrypted and then later become encrypted.

The functional tests where the `deprecatedrpc` argument is added are
ones where functionality or behavior of `encryptwallet` is being tested,
they should be kept until the RPC command is removed.
